The utilization and user figures are as of December 2025, about 11 months old. The report should label them as end-of-2025 figures, not current status.
missing_perspectives: The brief asks what problems came up, but the draft covers only payment-terminal faults. It does not state that the 92% availability means about 8% downtime, and it does not say the notes contain no other problem data (user complaints, siting, grid constraints, vandalism).
There is no benchmark or interpretation for 31% utilization or 92% uptime, so the reader cannot tell whether the pilot succeeded. Note that the sources give no targets or comparisons.
Cost is not set against outcomes, for example about 633 dollars per registered user. Revenue, tariffs and energy delivered are also not covered, and the report should say these are unknown.
Two of the four sources are council or city documents, with only the reliability audit independent. The draft does not flag this.
suggested_revisions: Change to '4,900 residents registered as regular users'.
Add 'installation' to the cost sentence and give the 'fewer than 20%' threshold for phase two.
Expand the problems section: 'Chargers were unavailable about 8% of the time, with payment-terminal faults behind 63% of reported outages; the sources do not document other issues.'
Add a sentence noting the absence of targets or benchmarks for utilization and uptime, and that the figures date from December 2025.

unsupported_claims: The claim that listings rose 'mainly because investors sold rental homes' appears in none of the notes. Source [1] reports only the listing count and the year-over-year change, with no cause.
Citation [4] (Homebuyer Pulse) does not appear in the research notes. Nothing in the notes backs any claim attributed to it.
factual_concerns: Days on market is misstated. The dashboard says 18 to 27 days (June 2025 to June 2026). The draft says 18 to 37 days.
The time periods are mixed without saying so. Price and listings are Q2 year-over-year figures. Days on market and months of supply are June-only comparisons. The draft does not mark this difference.
missing_perspectives: The mortgage rate data is left out. The average 30-year fixed rate fell from 6.9% to 6.4% (June 2025 to June 2026). Source [3] is listed but never used, and the rate drop is relevant context for prices rising while inventory grows.

There is no synthesis of the overall picture. Prices kept rising, but supply grew and homes sold more slowly, which points to a market cooling or rebalancing. The notes support that framing as long as it is not overstated.
suggested_revisions: Correct days on market to 'rose from 18 to 27 days (June 2025 to June 2026)'.
Delete the investor-selling explanation, or replace it with a sourced cause.
Remove citation [4] and cite only [2] for days on market and months of supply.
Add a sentence on mortgage rates citing [3]: 6.9% falling to 6.4%.
Label the time frames explicitly: Q2 year-over-year for price and listings, June-to-June for the dashboard metrics.

factual_concerns: Days on market and months of supply are stated without dates. The notes specify June 2025 vs June 2026 single-month snapshots; as written, they read as annual or Q2 figures.
'versus 6.9% in 2025' implies a 2025 average. The notes give 6.9% as the June 2025 figure ('a year earlier'), and it is the rate 'offered to' buyers, not rates actually obtained.
The title and framing ('2025 to 2026') overstate coverage. The evidence is only Q2 (prices, listings) and June (DOM, supply, rates) comparisons, not full-year changes.
missing_perspectives: No caveat that the sources use different periods and geographies. Q2 realtor data, a June county dashboard, and a regional ('midstate') lending survey may not align exactly.
The price figure covers single-family homes only. The listings count may cover a different property mix, and the draft doesn't flag this.

No synthesis for the research question. Prices still rose while inventory, supply and DOM all increased, which points to a cooling but still-appreciating market. The draft lists facts without stating this direction of change.
No mention of data gaps: sales volume, other property types, inflation-adjusted prices, and second-half 2026 trends.
The rate decline is not connected to the market shift, and the notes cannot establish causation. Keep it as context only.
suggested_revisions: Change to 'median days on market rose from 18 in June 2025 to 27 in June 2026; months of supply rose from 2.1 to 2.9 over the same period [2].'
Change the rate sentence to '6.4% in June 2026 versus 6.9% in June 2025 (average rate offered, regional lending survey) [3].'
Add a one-sentence summary: prices up modestly (+4.2%), while inventory (+19%), months of supply and time on market all rose, indicating a cooling market with continued price growth.
Add a brief limitations line covering mixed time windows (Q2 vs June), single-family-only pricing, the regional rate survey, and the lack of full-year data.
Retitle or scope the report as 'Q2/June 2025 vs 2026' rather than implying full-year coverage.

F6.quote: The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate offered to Kestrel County buyers was 6.4% in June 2026, compared with 6.9% a year earlier.

F1.text: The figure '21%' in the report contradicts the notes, which give 11%.

F6.text: The statement containing '40 million' is not supported by the research notes.

F4.quote: Operators that moved to direct liquid cooling cut average power usage effectiveness (PUE) from 1.38 to 1.12 across 23 surveyed sites.

F5.quote: AI training and inference clusters accounted for 58% of that data center load.

unsupported_claims: 'saving operators 40 million dollars a year' has no basis in the notes. The cooling survey reports only the PUE change (1.38 to 1.12 across 23 sites) and gives no cost or savings figures.
Citation [4] (Green Compute Index) does not appear in the research notes. It cannot support the 14.2 TWh / 58% claim, and its content is unverified.
factual_concerns: The draft says data centers used 21% of the grid's electricity. The annual review says 11%, so this misstatement roughly doubles the share.
The draft attributes the PUE figure to 'sites that switched' in general. The figure is an average across 23 surveyed sites, not across all operators on the grid.

The opening calls the load 'AI data center electricity', but 14.2 TWh is total data center load. AI clusters are only 58% of it, about 8.2 TWh. The draft never states the AI-specific figure that the question asks for.
missing_perspectives: The 2030 outlook (24 TWh central forecast, about a 69% rise from 14.2 TWh) is listed as source [3] but never used. It is needed to show the trend and the context of growth.

The draft does not say that lower PUE cuts cooling and overhead energy, not the IT/compute load itself. The roughly 19% cut in total facility energy at the same IT load is an inference from the PUE change and should be labeled as one.
The notes contain no other reduction measures (efficiency of chips or models, load shifting, heat reuse). The draft should say this evidence gap openly rather than imply cooling is the full answer.
There are no caveats about the scope of the survey: 23 sites, possible self-selection, and no information on how many Norrland sites have adopted liquid cooling.
suggested_revisions: Change 21% to 11%, matching [1].
Remove citation [4] and its source entry, and cite only [1] for the 14.2 TWh and 58% figures.
Delete the '40 million dollars a year' claim, or replace it with a sourced figure.
Add the derived AI-specific load (about 8.2 TWh, 58% of 14.2 TWh) and label it as a calculation.
Add the 24 TWh 2030 forecast from [3] and note that it is a central forecast.
Qualify the PUE result as an average across 23 surveyed sites, and explain that it reduces overhead energy rather than compute energy.

factual_concerns: The draft never answers the core question: how much electricity AI data centers use. From the notes, AI clusters' load is 58% × 14.2 TWh ≈ 8.2 TWh (about 6.4% of grid electricity). The draft leaves readers to infer this.
The 14.2 TWh covers the year to June 2026, not calendar 2026. The draft states the period correctly, but it should flag that this is the closest available figure rather than a full 2026 total.
'Sites that switched…' reads as if it covers all switching operators. The notes say this is an average across 23 surveyed sites only.

The PUE drop from 1.38 to 1.12 reduces facility overhead, not IT load. It implies roughly 19% less total facility energy for the same IT load (1.12/1.38 ≈ 0.81). The draft gives no energy or TWh translation, so its practical scale is unclear.

The 2030 figure is described simply as what the operator 'expects'. The notes call it the 'central forecast', so the draft drops the scenario framing. It also covers all data centers, not AI specifically.
missing_perspectives: The notes do not say whether the 23 surveyed sites are AI facilities, so the link between the cooling finding and AI load is unestablished. The draft implies a connection it cannot support.
Only one efficiency measure, liquid cooling, is covered. The 'how are operators cutting it' part of the brief is thinly answered and should be acknowledged as a limitation of the evidence.
There is no context on growth: 14.2 → 24 TWh is about +69% by 2030, which suggests efficiency gains are being outpaced by demand.
The survey may be self-selected (operators reporting successful retrofits). This caveat is absent.
suggested_revisions: Add an explicit AI figure: 'AI training and inference clusters used roughly 8.2 TWh (58% of 14.2 TWh), about 6% of Norrland grid electricity, in the year to June 2026 [1].'

Reword the cooling claim: 'Across 23 surveyed sites, operators that moved to direct liquid cooling cut average PUE from 1.38 to 1.12 [2], roughly 19% less total energy for the same computing load.' Note that the survey does not specify whether these were AI sites.
Change the forecast sentence to 'The operator's central forecast has total data center demand reaching 24 TWh by 2030 (about 69% above the 2026 level) [3].'
Add a brief limitations line: the evidence covers only cooling retrofits, there is no AI-specific forecast, and the period is a mid-year to mid-year span.

unsupported_claims: 'Adding emojis to subject lines doubles open rates' has no source in the notes and no citation. It is also especially unreliable given that the notes say opens are inflated by machine opens.
Citation [4] (Email Marketing Almanac) does not appear in the research notes, so the benchmark figures cannot be checked against it.
factual_concerns: The report says the plain-text lift was 48%, but source [3] reports an 18% lift in click rate. This misstates the source's figure.
The benchmarks cover only the first half of 2026 across 1,400 newsletters. The report should not present them as typical for all of 2026, and it should state the sample.

The report should say that 41% is a reported open rate inflated by machine opens. It does not adjust that figure for the estimated 35% machine opens, which would bring it to about 27%. That adjustment is a rough inference and should be labeled as one.
missing_perspectives: The send-time finding is omitted. Tuesday-morning sends lifted click rate by 6% compared with Friday afternoons, across 212 controlled tests. The brief asks which changes improved results, and this is one of them.
The report gives no context on the tests, such as that there were 212 controlled tests and that the lifts are relative rather than percentage points (18% of 2.3% is roughly 2.7%).
The report does not note that median figures hide variance, and that the medians are self-reported.
suggested_revisions: Change 48% to 18% and attribute it to the 212 controlled tests [3].
Delete the emoji claim, or find a source for it and cite it.
Remove citation [4] or replace it with a source from the notes, and cite only [1] for the benchmarks.
Add the Tuesday-morning versus Friday-afternoon result: a 6% click lift [3].
State that the benchmarks cover H1 2026 across 1,400 newsletters. Clarify that the lifts are relative, and give a rough click rate implied by the 18% lift.
Put click rate first as the primary benchmark, given the open-rate inflation.

unsupported_claims: No sentence lacks support, but the draft drops the hedge on machine opens. The notes call the 35% figure 'the study estimates'. Applying it across the board implies it holds for the 1,400-newsletter benchmark sample, which the notes do not establish.
Calling plain-text 'newsletters' an improvement over 'designed templates' generalizes slightly. The notes say 'heavily designed templates', so the comparison is narrower than the draft implies.
factual_concerns: The 18% and 6% lifts are almost certainly relative, not percentage-point, increases. The draft does not say so, and a reader could take them as +18 points on a 2.3% baseline. As relative lifts they mean roughly 2.3% → 2.7% and 2.3% → 2.4%.
The title and framing say '2026 benchmarks', but the data covers only H1 2026. The body notes this once; the headline overstates the coverage.
The draft does not say whether the open and click rates are self-reported. It also does not say whether click rate is clicks/delivered or clicks/opens, which changes how the numbers should be read.
missing_perspectives: There is no distribution (quartiles or range) around the medians, so the reader cannot judge what a 'good' newsletter looks like.
The draft does not estimate privacy-adjusted opens (41% × 0.65 ≈ 27%), with a caveat that the 35% figure comes from a separate study.
Bot or security-scanner clicks may also inflate click rates. This weakens the claim that click rate is 'more reliable' and should be acknowledged as a limitation.
Source [3] is titled 'Subject line and send-time tests', yet the draft reports no subject-line findings. It should either report them or state that the notes contain none.
The draft does not say whether the 212 tests were specifically on B2B software senders, or how large and consistent the effects were across tests.
It does not acknowledge that 'which changes improved them' is answered with only two interventions, from a single source.
suggested_revisions: Rewrite the lifts explicitly, e.g. 'an 18% relative lift in click rate (roughly 2.3% to 2.7% at the median)'.
Retitle to 'H1 2026', or state in the opening line that full-year data is not available.
Add a sentence on the implied adjusted open rate (~27%). Caveat that the 35% machine-open estimate comes from a different study and may not match the benchmark sample.
Say 'heavily designed templates' to match the source.
Add a short limitations section covering self-reported medians, no spread data, single-source intervention evidence, possible bot clicks, and the undefined click-rate denominator.
Address the absence of subject-line results from source [3].

unsupported_claims: 'The program will be rolled out nationally in 2027' does not appear in any source in the notes.
Citation [4] (Health Systems Weekly) is not among the research notes, so it cannot support the cost figure. The cost claim rests only on [3].
factual_concerns: The draft says waits fell to 2.8 hours. The evaluation [1] says 3.8 hours. This misstatement inflates the drop from 0.8 to 1.8 hours.

The draft implies the clinics caused the whole fall in waits. Waits in the comparison regions without clinics also fell, from 4.5 to 4.3 hours, so the difference-in-differences effect is about 0.6 hours, not the full drop.
The 71% figure comes from self-reported counterfactual intent. It is not observed diversion, and the draft presents it without that caveat.
missing_perspectives: The draft leaves out the comparison-region data from the evaluation, which is the key evidence on whether the clinics caused the change.

It does not answer the 'at what cost' question in terms of value. It gives no cost per avoided ED visit and no comparison with what an ED visit costs, and the notes contain no ED cost data. The draft should state that gap.
It does not note limits on the evidence: only six months of data, possible seasonal effects, and an evaluation produced by the health board that runs the program.
suggested_revisions: Change '2.8 hours' to '3.8 hours'.
Add: 'In two neighbouring regions without clinics, waits fell from 4.5 to 4.3 hours, suggesting the clinics account for roughly 0.6 hours of the reduction.'
Delete the national rollout sentence, or source it.
Remove citation [4], or add Health Systems Weekly to the evidence base.
Qualify the 71% as self-reported. Optionally state that the implied cost is about 9.4M / ~36,900 self-reported diverted visits ≈ 255 per diverted visit, and that no ED cost comparison is available.
Specify the currency for the 9.4 million and the 181 per visit.

unsupported_claims: No claim goes beyond the notes; every figure (4.6→3.8 h, 4.5→4.3 h, 52,000 visits, 71%, 9.4 million, ~181 per visit) matches its cited source. 9.4M / 52,000 ≈ 180.8, so 'about 181' is consistent.
factual_concerns: By placing the two trends side by side, the draft implies the clinics caused the drop without saying so. Neighboring regions are a non-randomized comparison, so the notes support only an association, not a proven causal effect.
The 71% 'would otherwise have gone to an ED' figure is a self-reported counterfactual. It likely overstates true diversion, and the draft presents it without caveat.
The data cover only January–June 2026, but the question asks about 2026. Full-year effects are unknown, and the draft does not flag this.
The currency for 9.4 million and 181 per visit is unspecified in both notes and draft.
missing_perspectives: There is no explicit answer to the question. The draft should state the comparison-adjusted effect: about 0.8 h drop vs 0.2 h in comparison regions, roughly 0.6 h (~36 min) relative reduction in median wait.

Cost is not tied to outcome. For example, about 181 per visit or roughly 255 per self-reported avoided ED visit (9.4M / ~36,900). The draft also omits any ED costs offset, which the notes do not provide; that gap should be acknowledged.
Evaluation independence is not addressed. The evaluation comes from the Health Board running the program, with no independent verification.
Possible confounders or differences between the valley and comparison regions are not discussed, such as baseline trends, staffing changes, or seasonality.
The draft says nothing about whether waits held steady after June or about the quality of clinic care.
suggested_revisions: Add a bottom-line opening sentence. For example: 'Evidence suggests the clinics were associated with a roughly 0.6-hour larger fall in median ED waits than comparison regions in H1 2026, at about 9.4 million (≈181 per visit).'
Add caveats: non-randomized comparison, self-reported diversion, a self-evaluation by the program operator, and six-month data only.
Report the difference-in-differences figure and a cost per avoided ED visit, and label it as an estimate based on self-reports.
Specify the currency, or note that the source does not state it.
State that no data on ED cost savings or full-year results are available.

# AI answer panels and retail organic clicks in 2026

Across 120,000 retail queries sampled in March 2026, Lumen Search showed an AI answer panel on 38% of queries, up from 21% in March 2025 [1]. Panels appeared most often on informational queries (61%) and least often on branded queries (9%) [1].

When a panel appeared, the first organic result's click-through rate fell by 27% compared with the same queries without a panel. Results cited inside the panel lost 8% of clicks [2]. Retail sites with product pages carrying structured price and availability data were cited in 44% of panels where they ranked in the top ten, compared with 17% for sites without that data [3].

SEO teams should track panel presence rate, citation share inside panels, and click-through rate split by panel present versus absent [4].

# Harrow Bay's curbside EV charging pilot

Harrow Bay installed 240 curbside chargers on light poles between February and June 2025. By December, utilization reached 31% of available hours, and 4,900 residents had registered as regular users [1].

The pilot cost 3.1 million dollars, or about 12,900 dollars per charger including installation and two years of maintenance [2].

Chargers were available 92% of the time; payment terminal faults caused 63% of reported outages [3]. The council approved a second phase of 600 chargers for 2026, prioritizing streets where fewer than 20% of homes have off-street parking [4].

# B2B software newsletter benchmarks, 2026

The median B2B software newsletter reported a 41% open rate and a 2.3% click rate in the first half of 2026 [1].

Open rates overstate engagement: an estimated 35% of recorded opens were automatic machine opens, so click rate is the more reliable measure [2].

Plain-text style newsletters lifted click rate by 18% over heavily designed templates. Sending on Tuesday mornings lifted click rate by 6% compared with Friday afternoons [3].

# Kestrel County housing, 2025 to 2026

The median single-family sale price reached 412,000 dollars in Q2 2026, up 4.2% from a year earlier, while active listings rose 19% to 2,180 [1].

Homes took longer to sell: median days on market rose from 18 days in June 2025 to 27 days in June 2026, and months of supply grew from 2.1 to 2.9 [2]. The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate offered to Kestrel County buyers was 6.4% in June 2026, down from 6.9% a year earlier [3].

# Ostrava Valley evening clinics and emergency waits

After six evening clinics opened in January 2026, the median emergency department wait in the valley fell from 4.6 hours to 3.8 hours by June [1]. In two neighboring regions without clinics, waits fell from 4.5 hours to 4.3 hours over the same period [1].

The clinics handled 52,000 visits in the first half of 2026, and 71% of patients said they would otherwise have gone to an emergency department [2].

Running costs were 9.4 million for the first six months, about 181 per visit [3].

# AI data center electricity on the Norrland grid

Data centers used 14.2 terawatt-hours in the year to June 2026, 11% of the grid’s electricity; AI training and inference clusters made up 58% of that load [1].

Across 23 surveyed sites, operators that moved to direct liquid cooling cut average PUE from 1.38 to 1.12 [2].

The grid operator’s central forecast has data center demand reaching 24 terawatt-hours by 2030 [3].
